analysis.one_liner: Extends Medicare's negotiated drug prices to private insurance and caps out-of-pocket drug costs.
analysis.headline: Introduced in November 2025 with 58 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party; the bill sits in three House committees with no hearing or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would lower prescription drug costs for people with private insurance. It would extend Medicare's negotiated "maximum fair prices" to group health plans and individual insurance, count drug makers' rising prices against them for commercial sales through inflation rebates, and cap what patients pay out of pocket — including $35-a-month insulin with no deductible. It would also let Medicare negotiators look at prices charged in six other wealthy countries and would undo parts of a 2025 budget law that changed the negotiation program. The bill has not moved since it was referred to three House committees.
analysis.who_benefits: People with employer-based or individual health insurance, especially anyone on expensive brand-name drugs or insulin. Negotiated prices would apply to their plans, their annual out-of-pocket drug spending would be capped at $2,000 for individual coverage (with an overall cap at roughly the 2014 Affordable Care Act limit, adjusted for inflation), and insulin would cost no more than $35 a month with no deductible, starting in 2027.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with private insurance on costly drugs

how_it_helps.text: The number of drugs Medicare negotiates each year would rise from 20 to 50, and negotiated prices would apply to group health plans and individual market coverage whose insurers do not opt out; patient cost-sharing would be calculated from the negotiated price, not the list price.
Medicare's inflation rebates — which force manufacturers to pay back amounts above inflation — would apply to drugs sold in the commercial market, not just to Medicare.
Negotiators would have to weigh the drug's average price in Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Japan, and the United Kingdom for negotiations starting in 2028.
The bill would repeal the changes to the negotiation program made by Public Law 119-21, the 2025 budget reconciliation law, restoring the program as it was before that law.

For plan years beginning in 2027, private coverage would have to cap annual prescription drug cost-sharing at $2,000 for self-only coverage, cap overall cost-sharing at the 2014 ACA out-of-pocket limit adjusted for premium growth, cover selected insulin at no more than $35 per 30-day supply with no deductible, and cover the essential health benefits package; plans offering coverage at any metal level would also have to offer a child-only plan.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would lose revenue from lower negotiated prices, inflation rebates on commercial sales, and international price benchmarks. Health insurers and the employers that sponsor group plans would absorb a share of costs that patients no longer pay at the pharmacy, which could push premiums up unless drug savings offset it.

drawbacks.text: Participation in the negotiated prices is technically voluntary: a health plan or insurer can elect not to participate for a given drug and year, and must publicly disclose the opt-out — so the reach of negotiated prices into the private market depends on plans choosing to stay in.

The cost-sharing caps and insulin mandate have no funding mechanism, so the costs that patients no longer pay would be shifted to insurers and employers and, if not offset by drug savings, into premiums.

The out-of-pocket limits and insulin requirement apply only to plan years beginning in 2027 or later, and the insulin cap covers each plan's selected insulin products rather than every insulin on the market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients with high drug costs, the benefits are direct and large: negotiated prices, a $2,000 annual drug cap, and $35 insulin. The main honest cost is that somebody must pay the difference, and this bill assigns it to drug makers and to insurers and employers through premium pressure without offsets. The voluntary opt-out also weakens the central mechanism — an insurer that expects to lose money on a negotiated drug can leave the program, though it would have to say so publicly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to three House committees; none has taken it up, and no hearing or vote is scheduled while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Representative Frank Pallone introduced the bill on November 20, 2025, with Representatives Richard Neal and Bobby Scott of Virginia joining as original sponsors.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce committees, and no further action is recorded.
Fifty-eight House Democrats have cosponsored the bill; no Republican has.
Because Congress is still in session, the bill could still receive committee action, but nothing is scheduled.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far nothing has changed: brand-name drug manufacturers and health insurers continue operating under current pricing rules, and patients' out-of-pocket drug costs are unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and insurers, for now

sides.party_line_note: All 59 sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill's fate rests with Republican-controlled committees.

industries.note: The bill subjects commercial sales of selected drugs to Medicare-negotiated maximum prices, applies inflation rebates to drugs sold outside Medicare, and requires negotiators to weigh prices in six other developed countries — all of which directly reduce what manufacturers can charge.

Insurers would pay lower prices for selected drugs but must cap what patients pay out of pocket and absorb the difference; they can opt out of negotiated prices for a given drug but must publish the opt-out. Whether their net interest is positive depends on whether drug savings cover the added cost-sharing obligation.

Group plans must comply with the new out-of-pocket caps and insulin coverage rules, shifting costs that patients previously paid onto employers and plan funding, unless lower negotiated drug prices offset it.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 223 House seats, no Republican cosponsor, and the bill sitting in three committees with no scheduled hearing, the realistic path is that it does not advance this Congress; drug-pricing bills of this scope have generally needed unified control of government to move.
